title: The internet lives at the bottom of the sea

lines: The message you just sent didn't go to space.
It went down. To the bottom of the ocean.
More than ninety-nine percent of data between continents travels through cables on the seafloor.
Laid end to end, they'd wrap the Earth more than forty times.
And in the deep ocean, each one is about as thick as a garden hose.
Inside, glass threads thinner than a hair carry your message as flashes of light.
You've probably seen a shark biting a cable.
But in the fault records from 2007 to 2014, fish caused exactly zero breaks.
The real culprits are fishing gear and ship anchors.
Around two hundred cable faults happen every year. That's three or four a week.
And only about sixty ships on Earth can fix them.
They drop a hook kilometers down, drag it across the seabed,
and haul the broken cable up into the daylight.
In 2024, cuts in the Red Sea disrupted about a quarter of the traffic between Europe and Asia.
So the next time a message arrives in a second,
remember the garden hose at the bottom of the sea.
